items.source: The electromotive force acting between two points is measured by the work done on a unit of positive electricity transferred from one point to the other.
items.explanation: **Electromotive force is really just a measure of push.** Imagine you have a tiny, imaginary ball carrying one unit of positive electric charge. You move that ball from one point to another inside an electric field. The amount of work the field does on that ball during the trip, meaning the energy it takes to push the ball along, is exactly what we call the electromotive force between those two points. So electromotive force is not some mysterious extra thing; it is simply a way of measuring how hard electricity is being pushed, by asking how much energy gets used when a standard amount of charge travels between two spots.

items.source: The electromotive force acting between two points is measured by the work done on a unit of positive electricity transferred from one point to the other.
items.explanation: Maxwell wrote this at a time when scientists were still arguing about what "electromotive force" actually was and how to pin it down with a number. The phrase "work done" is the key: work here means the same thing it means in a machine, the effort needed to push something from one place to another. Maxwell is saying you measure the push that electricity feels between two points by asking how much effort it would take to carry a tiny imaginary package of positive electricity from one point to the other. That gives you a real, countable number instead of a vague idea. It mattered because once you could measure the push that way, you could compare it, calculate with it, and build the rest of electrical theory on solid ground.

items.source: The electromotive force acting between two points is measured by the work done on a unit of positive electricity transferred from one point to the other.
items.explanation:
**Electromotive force** is the tricky one here. Today "force" makes you picture a push or a pull, something physical. But Maxwell uses it the way scientists of his time did: it just means the electrical pressure, or drive, that moves electricity from one place to another. It is not really a force you could feel with your hand. Think of it like water pressure pushing water through a pipe.

**Work done** is the other key phrase. Maxwell means something precise: how much energy gets used up moving a tiny fixed amount of electricity between two points. The "unit of positive electricity" is just a standard-sized package of charge, like a measuring cup, so the answer comes out the same every time you measure.

Put together, the sentence is saying: to find out how strong the electrical drive is between two spots, move that standard package from one spot to the other and measure the energy spent doing it. That energy spent is your answer.

items.source: The electromotive force acting between two points is measured by the work done on a unit of positive electricity transferred from one point to the other.
items.explanation: Think of electricity like water flowing through a pipe. The "electromotive force" is the push that makes the water move. Maxwell says we measure this push by doing a simple math trick: imagine moving a tiny, single drop of positive water from one spot to another. If you had to do a lot of work to push that drop, the force is strong. If it moved easily, the force is weak. So, the force is just the amount of effort needed to move that one unit of charge between two places. This matters because it turns an invisible push into a number we can count, letting us build better machines like motors and lights.

items.source: The electromotive force acting between two points is measured by the work done on a unit of positive electricity transferred from one point to the other.
items.explanation: This line explains how we measure the push that moves electricity. Imagine pushing a ball up a hill; the work you do is the energy you spend. Here, scientists measure that same effort but for a tiny piece of positive charge moving between two spots. The "electromotive force" is just the name for that push. If you move a unit of electricity from one place to another, the total work done tells you exactly how strong that push is. This matters because it turns an invisible force into a number we can count, letting us build better machines and understand how power flows through wires.

items.source: The electromotive force acting between two points is measured by the work done on a unit of positive electricity transferred from one point to the other.
items.explanation: The sentence says that the push of electricity, called electromotive force, is just a way of measuring how much work it takes to move a tiny bit of positive charge from one spot to another. Work here means the effort or energy used to push something against a force, like pushing a heavy box up a hill. A unit of positive electricity is just a very small, standard amount of electric charge, like a single grain of sand compared to a whole bucket. Transferred means moving from one place to another, just like passing a ball to a friend. So, instead of using a complicated machine to measure the push, we imagine moving this tiny bit of charge and see how much energy we had to spend. If it takes a lot of energy to move that tiny bit, the push is strong. If it takes very little energy, the push is weak. This simple idea lets us understand electricity by counting the effort needed to move charge, turning a hard-to-see force into something we can measure with work.

items.explanation: The flame is not just sitting there glowing. The melted wax is constantly being pulled up the wick and then broken apart by the heat into lighter substances, gases basically, that catch fire and give off that bright light you see. **The heat is doing two jobs at once:** it keeps the wax moving upward, and it also splits the wax apart into the stuff that actually burns and glows. So the bright part of the flame is not burning wax directly. It is burning the broken-down pieces of wax that the heat has already changed into something new.

items.source: The fluid part of the flame is continually rising and being consumed, and the heat decomposes the wax into substances that burn with that bright light.
items.explanation: Faraday was giving these talks at a time when most people thought fire was just fire, a simple thing that happened when something got hot enough. He wanted to show that a candle flame is actually a little machine with different parts doing different jobs. The word "decomposes" here means the heat breaks the wax apart into smaller, lighter substances, the way heat breaks an egg into something completely different from what you started with. So the wax does not just vanish into light; it first gets torn into pieces by the heat, and those pieces are what actually burn and glow. That idea, that burning is really a chain of changes happening one after another, was new and surprising to his audience, and it is why he keeps slowing down to show you each step.

items.source: The fluid part of the flame is continually rising and being consumed, and the heat decomposes the wax into substances that burn with that bright light.
items.explanation: **Decomposes** is the word doing the most work here. Faraday means the heat breaks the wax apart into smaller, lighter substances, the way heat can split one thing into several different things. Today we mostly hear "decompose" used for rotting, like a dead leaf breaking down in the soil. But Faraday uses it the chemistry way: heat forces the wax molecules, the tiny building blocks of wax, to come apart and turn into new substances. Those new substances are what actually catch fire and glow. So the wax itself is not really what burns bright. The heat first has to tear it apart, and then the pieces that come off burn with that strong white light. Without that breaking-apart step, you would get no flame at all.

items.source: The fluid part of the flame is continually rising and being consumed, and the heat decomposes the wax into substances that burn with that bright light.
items.explanation: The flame works like a busy factory inside the candle. The liquid wax melts and floats up to the top, where the heat breaks it apart into tiny pieces that can burn. This breaking apart is what Faraday calls "decomposing," which just means splitting something into smaller parts. When these small pieces mix with air, they catch fire and make the bright light we see. The heat is the worker that does the splitting, and the rising fluid is the fuel that keeps the worker busy. Without this constant rising and splitting, the candle would stop glowing. So the light comes from the heat breaking the wax into burnable bits that fly up to the flame.

items.source: The fluid part of the flame is continually rising and being consumed, and the heat decomposes the wax into substances that burn with that bright light.

Faraday explains this to show that the fire is not just a single thing but a process where the wax changes and moves. He answers the question of how the candle keeps burning by showing that the liquid wax rises and the heat turns it into burning gas. This mattered because it proved that fire needs fuel to keep going and that the fuel changes form as it burns.

The heat does the work of splitting the wax so it can burn. Without that heat breaking the wax, the liquid would just sit there and not make light. items.source: Digestion is the process by which the food we eat is reduced into a fluid capable of being absorbed and assimilated by the tissues of the body.
items.explanation: **Digestion turns solid food into a liquid the body can actually use.** Your body cannot pull goodness out of a chunk of bread or meat directly. It has to break that food all the way down into a thin fluid first. Once the food is in that liquid form, the tiny walls of your gut can soak it up, and then your body's tissues, meaning the actual flesh and organs that make you up, can take it in and use it to grow, repair, and keep running. Think of it like dissolving a sugar cube in water: the sugar only mixes into your drink once it stops being a solid lump.

items.source: Digestion is the process by which the food we eat is reduced into a fluid capable of being absorbed and assimilated by the tissues of the body.
items.explanation: By the 1850s and 1860s, most people still thought digestion was basically just the stomach grinding food up, like a mill. Lewes was writing for ordinary readers who had no science training, and he wanted to show that something more interesting was happening: food does not just get crushed, it gets chemically changed into a liquid that the body's own tissues can actually take in and use. The phrase "absorbed and assimilated" means the liquid soaks through the gut wall and then becomes part of your body's own flesh. That two-step idea, soaking in and then becoming part of you, was newer and more surprising than it sounds now, and it is the whole reason the rest of his chapter matters.

items.source: Digestion is the process by which the food we eat is reduced into a fluid capable of being absorbed and assimilated by the tissues of the body.
items.explanation: **Assimilated** is the word that needs unpacking here. Today we mostly use it to mean fitting into a new culture, but Lewes means something more physical: the tissues of your body actually take the digested food in and turn it into part of themselves, the way a sponge soaks up water and becomes wet all the way through. The food stops being food and becomes you. That one word carries the whole point of the sentence: digestion is not just breaking food down, it is the start of your body rebuilding itself out of what you ate.

items.source: Digestion is the process by which the food we eat is reduced into a fluid capable of being absorbed and assimilated by the tissues of the body.
items.explanation: Digestion is just the body's way of turning your food into a liquid soup so your cells can drink it up. Imagine you eat a big, hard apple. Your body cannot use that hard chunk directly, so it breaks it down into a watery mix. This mix is what your tissues need to get energy and grow. Without this step, the food would just sit there and do nothing. The writer is explaining that eating is only the first part; the real work happens inside you when everything turns into a fluid. **The body must turn solid food into liquid fuel before it can use it.** This is why you feel hungry again after a while; the liquid has been absorbed and used up.

items.source: Digestion is the process by which the food we eat is reduced into a fluid capable of being absorbed and assimilated by the tissues of the body.
items.explanation: Digestion is just the body's way of turning the food you eat into a liquid soup that your cells can drink up. Imagine you eat a big steak, but your body cannot use the solid meat directly. Instead, it breaks the steak down into tiny, watery pieces. This happens so your tissues can take in the nutrients they need to grow and stay strong. Without this process, the food would just sit in your stomach and do nothing. It is like a factory that crushes big rocks into fine sand so a machine can use the sand to build something new. The whole point is to change solid food into something soft enough to travel through your blood and reach every part of you.

items.source: Digestion is the process by which the food we eat is reduced into a fluid capable of being absorbed and assimilated by the tissues of the body.
items.explanation: The word "digestion" today often just means the stomach churning, but here it means breaking food down into a liquid soup so the body can use it. The word "absorbed" means the body taking that liquid into its parts, like a sponge soaking up water. The word "assimilated" means the body turning that liquid into its own flesh and blood, not just keeping it as a drink. The author is saying food is useless until it becomes a fluid that the body can actually take in and use to grow. If the food stays solid, the body cannot get the energy or building blocks it needs. So digestion is the first step of turning outside food into inside life. Without this turning into a liquid, we would starve even if we ate enough, because our tissues could not grab the nutrients. The whole point is that food must change form to become part of us.

items.source: The building called the panopticon is a circular prison so contrived that an inspector at the centre may survey every cell without himself being seen.
items.explanation: A circular prison where one guard in the middle can watch every prisoner, but no prisoner can see the guard. The tricky part is "contrived," which here means carefully designed on purpose, not accidental. The whole **power** of the building comes from that one-way watching: prisoners never know if they are being watched right now, so they must always act as if they are.

items.source: The building called the panopticon is a circular prison so contrived that an inspector at the centre may survey every cell without himself being seen.
items.explanation:
The key idea here is **you can be watched without knowing it**. Picture a round building shaped like a donut, with a guard tower in the middle. Every prison cell lines the outer ring, and each cell faces inward toward that tower. The guard in the middle can see into any cell at any moment. But the prisoners cannot see whether the guard is actually looking at them right now or not.

That matters because once you know you might be watched at any second, you start acting as if you are always being watched, even when no one is there. You police yourself. The building does the controlling, not just the guard. So the real power of this design is not the walls or the locks. It is the uncertainty, not knowing when eyes are on you, that keeps everyone in line all the time.

items.source: The building called the panopticon is a circular prison so contrived that an inspector at the centre may survey every cell without himself being seen.
items.explanation: Bentham wrote this in the late 1700s when prisons in Britain were filthy, chaotic places where guards had almost no real control. He wanted to show that a building's shape could do the work of dozens of watchmen. The key idea behind "may survey every cell without himself being seen" is that prisoners would never know exactly when they were being watched, so they would have to act as if they were always being watched. That constant uncertainty was supposed to keep order all by itself, without force. Bentham was pitching this to people who ran governments and paid for public buildings, trying to convince them that good design could replace expensive staff and brutal punishment.

items.source: The building called the panopticon is a circular prison so contrived that an inspector at the centre may survey every cell without himself being seen.
items.explanation: **Contrived** is the word doing the most work here. Today it sounds like something fake or forced, like a contrived excuse. But Bentham means it the older way: carefully designed and arranged on purpose. The building was not just built; it was worked out so that one specific thing would happen, that the guard in the middle could see every prisoner, but no prisoner could see the guard. That one-way watching is the whole point of the design, and "contrived" tells you it was planned down to the last detail to make it work.

items.source: The building called the panopticon is a circular prison so contrived that an inspector at the centre may survey every cell without himself being seen.
items.explanation: This building is a round prison where a guard stands in the middle to watch everyone. The trick is that the guard can see every single cell, but the prisoners cannot see him at all. This design makes the guard feel like he is watching you all the time, even if he is not actually looking at you right now. Because you never know when he might be peering through a window, you will start to act like you are being watched constantly. This means you will follow the rules and be very good on your own, without needing a guard to shout at you or lock you up. The whole point is that the fear of being seen changes your behavior, so you become your own best police officer.

items.source: The building called the panopticon is a circular prison so contrived that an inspector at the centre may survey every cell without himself being seen.
items.explanation: This passage describes a special prison called the panopticon, which is built in a circle so that a guard in the middle can watch every prisoner without them seeing him. The whole point is that the prisoners never know if they are being watched right now, so they act as if they always are. This trick makes them follow the rules on their own, without needing many guards. Bentham wanted to show how this design could control large groups of people cheaply and easily. It matters because it proves that just the idea of being watched can change how people behave, even if no one is actually looking at them at that moment.

items.source: The building called the panopticon is a circular prison so contrived that an inspector at the centre may survey every cell without himself being seen.
items.explanation: The word "contrived" is the hardest part here; it just means "designed in a special way." The author is saying the prison is built like a giant circle with cells around the outside and a guard tower in the middle. The special design lets the guard look out at every single room at once without anyone knowing he is watching. Today, if we say a plan is "contrived," we might think it is fake or forced. But in this old book, it simply means the building was made with a very clever trick. This trick changes everything because the prisoners never know if the guard is looking at them right now. They must act perfectly all the time because they might be watched. This makes them behave better not because they are nice, but because they are always afraid of being seen. The whole point of the building is that the guard can see everyone while staying hidden, which controls the people without him ever having to shout or move.
